screq_greer_2019_jcha.title: Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.
screq_greer_2019_jcha.citation: Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.

verification.note: Abstract read: the settler approach has much to offer, but across 500 years of invading Indigenous North America the settler variety dominates some periods and regions and fades in others. 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are other modes; extractivism has become predominant in recent decades. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes.

pe139_greer_pentland_1985.title: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.
pe139_greer_pentland_1985.citation: Allan Greer, “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland,” Labour/Le Travail 15 (Spring 1985): 7–22.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 7–22) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 2454, galley 2857; scanned with a text layer, also OCR'd locally; folios from the running heads). Passages used: Pentland's work is 'a fundamentally incoherent book' and 'neglects the broader context needed to grasp this general transformation' (p. 9); Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade' and 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9); subdivision of holdings resulted from 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16); Pentland's ethnic argument belongs to 'an ambivalent but, in the end, predominantly liberal, view of the advent of capitalism' (p. 18); 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' and 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19; n. 16 cites Paquet and Wallot 1972 for the commercial view); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); Pentland's neglect of the household economy 'inevitably leads him to write women out of his history' (p. 20); 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20); subsistence producers 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland' (p. 21). Note 2 (p. 8) discusses Kealey's and Palmer's readings of Pentland, calling Palmer's Working-Class Experience an 'otherwise excellent synthesis'. Note 14 announces Peasant, Lord and Merchant as forthcoming.

pe139_greer_pentland_1985.scope_note: Greer in his own words on the pre-capitalist household economy of early Canada, the transition to capitalism and the staples tradition.
